note: The days that aren't Tuesday. Holiday tables, cookouts, potlucks, bake sales, game days, and the fifteen-minute dinners for nights when cooking is the last thing anyone wants to do. Same rule as everywhere else: the base feeds everyone, and meat is an addition rather than the foundation.

recipes.title: Harvest Stuffed Acorn Squash
recipes.blurb: A centerpiece that doesn't apologize for not being a turkey. Roasted squash halves filled with wild rice, mushrooms, apples and pecans, glossed with cider.
steps: Heat oven to 400°F. Rub the cut faces of the squash with 2 tbsp oil and salt, lay them cut-side down on a sheet pan, and roast 35-40 minutes until a knife slides into the flesh with no resistance. Cut-side down is what caramelizes the rims.
Meanwhile simmer the wild rice in the broth, covered, 45 minutes until the grains split open. Drain any excess.
Brown the mushrooms in 2 tbsp oil over medium-high, undisturbed for 4 minutes, then tossing. Add onion and celery; cook 8 minutes. Add apple, garlic, sage and thyme for 2 minutes more.
Pour in the cider and let it cook away almost completely, scraping the pan. Fold in the rice, pecans, cranberries, salt and pepper.
Flip the squash halves, mound the filling in, and return to the oven for 12 minutes.
Finish with parsley. Serve each person half a squash — it looks like a plated course because it is one.

omnivore.label: Add sausage to half the filling
omnivore.note: Brown it separately and fold it into half the pan, so the vegetarian halves stay vegetarian.
steps: Brown the sausage 7 minutes, breaking it up, and fold into half the filling before stuffing. Mark those halves.

recipes.kidTweak: Kids often want the squash plain. Scoop out a half, mash it with a little maple, and serve the filling on the side as 'rice with cranberries in it'.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Fry 8 whole sage leaves in olive oil for 20 seconds until translucent and crisp, and lay two on each half. It takes a minute and it is the thing people photograph.
recipes.garden: Acorn squash stores until February in a cool room. Sage is a perennial here and will be waiting for you every autumn.
recipes.leftovers: Filling and squash both keep 4 days. Reheat covered at 350°F. The filling is excellent stirred into eggs.
recipes.prepAhead: Roast the squash and make the filling a day ahead; stuff and bake for 20 minutes before dinner. This is the one that saves a holiday.

recipes.title: Skillet Green Beans with Toasted Almonds
recipes.blurb: The green bean dish that replaces the casserole. Ten minutes, one pan, no canned soup, and it tastes like green beans on purpose.
steps: Boil the beans in well-salted water for 4 minutes, then drop them into ice water. This can happen the morning of — it is the whole reason this dish is calm on a holiday.
Toast the almonds in a dry skillet over medium, 3 minutes, until they smell nutty. Tip them out.
Warm the oil with the shallots over medium, 4 minutes, until soft and just golden. Add garlic and pepper flakes for 45 seconds.
Add the drained beans and toss over high heat 2-3 minutes until hot and blistered in places.
Off heat: salt, pepper, lemon juice and the almonds. Serve immediately, while the almonds are still loud.
recipes.kidTweak: Pull a handful of plain blanched beans before the garlic goes in. Cold blanched green beans are a genuinely popular kid snack.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Blanch and shock. Bright green beans on a holiday table, among a sea of beige, do more work than any garnish.
recipes.garden: Green beans in July freeze well after blanching — this is what to do with them in November.
recipes.leftovers: 3 days. Good cold, chopped into a salad.
recipes.prepAhead: Blanch up to 24 hours ahead, refrigerate in a towel-lined container, finish in 5 minutes.

recipes.title: Proper Herb Stuffing
recipes.blurb: Crisp on top, custardy underneath, and built on real bread and real herbs. It is a side dish, not an afterthought.
steps: Dry the bread: torn pieces on a sheet pan overnight on the counter, or 25 minutes at 275°F. Fresh bread makes paste, not stuffing.
Cook the onion and celery in the oil and butter over medium for 12 minutes until completely soft and sweet. Add garlic, sage and thyme for 2 minutes.
Whisk the broth with the eggs, salt and pepper.

Toss bread, vegetables and parsley in a big bowl, pour the custard over, and fold until every piece is damp but not collapsing. Let it sit 10 minutes and check — add another half cup of broth if the bottom of the bowl is dry.
Press into an oiled 9x13, cover with foil, and bake at 375°F for 30 minutes. Uncover and bake 25 more until the top is deeply browned and crisp.
Rest 10 minutes. The contrast between the crust and the soft middle is the entire dish, so do not stir it.

omnivore.label: Add browned sausage
omnivore.note: Fold into half the dish before baking if you want both versions.
steps: Brown 8 minutes and fold into half the bread mixture before it goes into the dish.

recipes.kidTweak: This is usually the dish kids like best. No changes needed.
recipes.restaurantTouch: A full teaspoon of black pepper. Stuffing is traditionally underseasoned and it is why it needs gravy to be interesting.
recipes.garden: Sage, thyme and parsley — the three herbs that survive an Ohio autumn and taste like the holiday.
recipes.leftovers: 4 days. Cut a square, fry it in a little oil until crisp, top with a fried egg. Better than the original.
recipes.prepAhead: Assemble unbaked a day ahead and refrigerate. Add 10 minutes to the covered bake.

recipes.title: Real Cranberry Sauce with Orange
recipes.blurb: Twelve minutes, four ingredients, and half the sugar of the canned version. The one dish where homemade is not just better, it is faster.
steps: Put everything except the zest in a saucepan with 2 tbsp water. Bring to a simmer over medium.
Cook 10-12 minutes, stirring occasionally. The berries will pop audibly — that is the sound of it working.
Pull it while about a quarter of the berries are still whole. It thickens a lot as it cools, so it should look slightly loose in the pan.
Stir in the orange zest off the heat. Cool completely before serving.
recipes.kidTweak: Kids who claim to hate cranberry sauce usually mean the ridged cylinder. Let them taste this one warm off the spoon.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Zest at the end, never at the start. Simmering drives off the aromatic oils that make it taste like oranges.
recipes.garden: Nothing — but buy an extra bag of cranberries in November and freeze it. They cook from frozen and keep a year.
recipes.leftovers: 2 weeks refrigerated. Swirl it into yogurt, or spread it on a sandwich with sharp cheddar.
recipes.prepAhead: Make it three days ahead and take one thing off the holiday-morning list.

recipes.title: Whipped Sweet Potatoes with Brown Butter and Sage
recipes.blurb: No marshmallows, no casserole. Just sweet potatoes tasting like themselves, with nutty brown butter and crisp sage on top.
steps: Roast the sweet potatoes whole at 400°F for 50-60 minutes until they collapse and leak syrup. Roasting rather than boiling concentrates them instead of waterlogging them — it is the difference between this and every sweet potato dish you have been served.
Scoop the flesh into a bowl. Mash or pulse with warm milk, yogurt, maple, salt and pepper until smooth.

Brown the butter: melt it in a small pan over medium and keep going past the foaming stage, swirling, 3-4 minutes, until the milk solids turn hazelnut brown and it smells like toffee. Watch it — it goes from brown to burnt in seconds.
Drop the sage leaves into the hot butter for 20 seconds until crisp.
Spread the potatoes in a wide dish, pour the brown butter over in a spiral, and scatter the sage and pecans.
recipes.kidTweak: Hold back a scoop before the pepper and serve it plain with a little extra maple.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Brown butter. Three extra minutes and it turns a familiar dish into one people ask about.
recipes.garden: Sweet potatoes grow well here from slips planted in June, and store for months.
recipes.leftovers: 4 days. Thin with milk and reheat gently; excellent under a fried egg.
recipes.prepAhead: Mash up to two days ahead. Reheat covered at 325°F and make the brown butter fresh — it takes four minutes.

recipes.title: Mushroom and Lentil Wellington
recipes.blurb: The showstopper. A deeply savory mushroom-lentil filling wrapped in pastry, sliced at the table to an actual audible reaction.

ingredients.prep: or a sheet of puff pastry

steps: Cook the mushrooms in 2 tbsp oil in a wide skillet over medium-high. They will release a shocking amount of water; keep going, 15-18 minutes, until the pan is dry and they have gone deep brown. This step cannot be rushed and it is the whole dish.
Add onion and the last tablespoon of oil; 6 minutes. Add garlic and thyme, 1 minute. Deglaze with the wine and cook it away entirely.
Wilt the spinach in the pan, then tip everything onto a board and chop it once more. Squeeze out any remaining liquid in a towel — a wet filling means a soggy bottom.
Mix with lentils, walnuts, panko, soy sauce, salt and pepper. Cool completely; warm filling steams the pastry from inside.
Roll the dough into a 12x14 rectangle. Mound the filling down the middle in a tight log, fold the sides over, seal, and roll it seam-side down onto a parchment-lined pan.
Brush with egg, score the top in shallow diagonals, and bake at 400°F for 35-40 minutes until deep golden.
Rest 10 minutes before slicing, or it falls apart. Serve in thick slices.
recipes.kidTweak: Bake a few small hand-pies from the same filling and trimmings. Kids will eat a pastry parcel they wouldn't touch on a plate.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Chill the assembled log for 20 minutes before it goes in the oven. Cold pastry into a hot oven is how you get layers.
recipes.garden: Thyme from the garden; the rest is a shopping trip.
recipes.leftovers: 3 days. Reheat slices at 375°F on a rack so the base re-crisps.
recipes.prepAhead: Make the filling two days ahead. Assemble the morning of and refrigerate; bake straight from cold, adding 5 minutes.

recipes.title: Winter Citrus and Fennel Salad
recipes.blurb: Bright, cold and crunchy against a table of rich food. Ten minutes, and it is the plate everyone goes back to.
steps: Cut the top and bottom off each citrus, stand it up, and cut the peel away in strips following the curve. Slice into rounds. Do it over the bowl so the juice lands in the dressing.
Soak the shaved onion in cold water for 10 minutes and drain — it takes the harshness out and leaves the crunch.
Arrange citrus and fennel in overlapping layers on a wide platter. Scatter onion and olives.
Dress with oil, vinegar, salt and pepper. Finish with pomegranate and mint.
Serve within the hour, at room temperature, so the citrus tastes of something.
recipes.kidTweak: Set aside a bowl of plain orange rounds and pomegranate seeds. That is a fruit salad and it will disappear.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Layer it flat on a platter rather than tossing it in a bowl. This is a dish you compose, and it takes the same amount of time.
recipes.garden: Fennel sown in July heads up here in October. Mint lives in a pot by the door.
recipes.leftovers: Best the day it is made; the fennel softens overnight.
recipes.heartNote: Grapefruit interacts with several common medications, including some statins. If that applies at your table, use all oranges — the dish loses nothing.

recipes.title: Hoppin' John
recipes.blurb: Black-eyed peas, rice and smoke — the New Year's Day pot that is supposed to bring luck, and definitely brings a cheap, excellent dinner.
steps: Cook onion, celery and pepper in the oil over medium for 10 minutes — this trio is the backbone, so let it soften properly.
Add garlic, smoked paprika, thyme and pepper flakes; 1 minute. The smoked paprika is doing the job a ham hock used to.
Add rice, broth, bay leaf and salt. Cover and simmer 30 minutes until the rice is tender.
Fold in the black-eyed peas and kale, cover, and cook 6 minutes more until the greens are silky.
Off heat: vinegar and scallions. The splash of vinegar at the end is traditional and it is what keeps a pot of beans from tasting flat.

omnivore.label: Add smoked turkey
omnivore.note: Traditional, and it makes the pot non-vegetarian — so brown it separately and add to bowls if that matters at your table.
steps: Brown with a teaspoon of smoked paprika and spoon over individual bowls.

recipes.kidTweak: Serve theirs before the pepper flakes go in, with the greens on the side.
recipes.restaurantTouch: A dash of hot sauce and a pile of scallions per bowl. In the South this is not a garnish, it is the dish.
recipes.garden: Kale is still standing in the garden on New Year's Day if you mulched it.
recipes.leftovers: 5 days, and it freezes for 3 months. Better on day two.
recipes.source: ERRERLabs original, after the Lowcountry classic

recipes.title: Black Bean Burgers That Hold Together
recipes.blurb: The two failures of a bean burger are mush and blandness. Roasting the beans first fixes both. These grill without a cage and taste like something you'd order.
steps: Spread the rinsed beans on a sheet pan and roast at 350°F for 15 minutes until the skins split and they look dry. This is the step everyone skips and it is why their burgers are mush.
Meanwhile cook the mushrooms and onion in 2 tbsp oil over medium-high, 10 minutes, until browned and dry. Add garlic, cumin, smoked paprika and chipotle for 1 minute.
Pulse two thirds of the beans in a processor to a coarse paste — not smooth. Mix with the whole beans, the mushroom mixture, panko, egg and salt.
Form 6 patties, pressing a shallow dimple into the center of each so they cook flat. Chill at least 30 minutes; this is not optional.
Grill over medium-hot, oiled grates 4-5 minutes a side without moving them, or sear in a skillet in the last tablespoon of oil.
Build on toasted buns with yogurt thinned with lime, avocado, tomato, red onion, lettuce and pickles.

omnivore.label: Grill burgers alongside
omnivore.note: Different zone of the grill, or a second skillet.
steps: Season and grill 5-6 minutes a side to 165°F.

recipes.kidTweak: Make a few slider-sized patties. Small food is more persuasive than a burger a kid can't get their mouth around.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Toast the buns cut-side down on the grill for 30 seconds. An untoasted bun goes soggy before the second bite.
recipes.garden: Tomatoes, lettuce and red onion straight from the beds in August.
recipes.leftovers: Cooked patties keep 4 days. Uncooked patties freeze 3 months between parchment — cook from frozen, adding 3 minutes a side.
recipes.prepAhead: Form the patties a day ahead. They improve overnight.

recipes.title: Grilled Vegetable Platter with Charred Scallion Sauce
recipes.blurb: The vegetable dish that stops being a side. Everything hits the grill, then gets piled on a platter under a bright green sauce.
steps: Heat the grill hot. Toss all the vegetables with 3 tbsp oil and half the salt.
Grill the whole bunch of scallions first, 3 minutes, until charred and floppy. Set aside — they are the sauce.
Grill everything else in batches: peppers and onions 4-5 minutes a side, zucchini and eggplant 3-4, asparagus 3. Do not crowd the grate and do not fuss with them.
Blend the charred scallions with garlic, parsley, lemon juice, vinegar, pepper flakes, the remaining 3 tbsp oil and the rest of the salt until coarse and vividly green.
Pile the vegetables on a big platter — warm or room temperature, not hot — and spoon the sauce over. Feta if you want it.

omnivore.label: Add chicken skewers or shrimp
omnivore.note: Same grill, same sauce, cooked after the vegetables come off.
steps: Toss in oil, salt and pepper flakes; grill 10-12 minutes turning, to 165°F. Serve alongside with the same sauce.

recipes.kidTweak: Grilled peppers and zucchini are sweet enough that most kids eat them plain. Keep a corner of the platter sauce-free.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Room temperature, not hot. Grilled vegetables taste more of themselves once they have settled for twenty minutes, which also means you are not cooking while guests arrive.
recipes.garden: This is the August garden on a platter.
recipes.leftovers: 4 days. Chop into a grain bowl, or layer into a sandwich with the leftover sauce.
recipes.prepAhead: Grill in the morning, sauce in the morning, assemble at room temperature before people arrive.

recipes.title: Crunchy Picnic Slaw, No Mayo
recipes.blurb: Sits out on a table for three hours without anyone worrying. Sharper and crunchier than the creamy kind, and it gets better as it sits.
steps: Slice the cabbage as thin as you can manage. Thickness is the whole texture of a slaw, and a sharp knife beats a food processor here.
Salt the cabbage and let it sit 15 minutes, then squeeze out the water. This is what keeps it crunchy on day three instead of watery by lunchtime.
Whisk oil, vinegar, Dijon, maple, cumin and pepper.
Toss everything except the pepitas. Let it sit at least 20 minutes before serving.
Add the pumpkin seeds right before it goes on the table so they stay crisp.
recipes.kidTweak: Set aside plain grated carrot and cabbage with a little dressing on the side.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Salt-and-squeeze the cabbage. It is fifteen unattended minutes and it is the difference between slaw and coleslaw soup.
recipes.garden: Cabbage, carrots, peppers and cilantro — a whole dish out of one bed.
recipes.leftovers: 4 days and genuinely good the whole time, which no mayonnaise slaw can claim.
recipes.prepAhead: Make it the day before. It improves.
recipes.heartNote: A vinaigrette slaw runs roughly a quarter of the sodium and a third of the saturated fat of a standard mayonnaise-based one.

recipes.title: Grilled Corn with Chili, Lime and Cotija-Style Crumble
recipes.blurb: Ohio sweet corn, charred hard, rolled in lime and chili. Fifteen minutes and it is the first thing to disappear.
steps: Heat the grill hot. Rub the corn with oil.
Grill 8-10 minutes, turning every couple of minutes, until charred in patches on every side. You want actual black, not golden — that char is the flavor.
Stir the yogurt with the juice of one lime and a pinch of salt.
Brush the hot corn with the lime yogurt, then roll it in the feta mixed with chili powder and smoked paprika.
Cilantro over the top, remaining lime cut into wedges. Serve immediately and provide napkins.
recipes.kidTweak: Grill a few ears plain and serve with nothing but a little butter and salt. Corn on the cob does not need help to be a kid's favorite.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Char it more than feels right. Timid corn is boiled corn with grill marks.
recipes.garden: Ohio sweet corn from a roadside stand in August is genuinely a different vegetable from what a supermarket sells in March.
recipes.leftovers: Cut the kernels off and fold them into salad, eggs or the corn-and-zucchini skillet.

recipes.title: Watermelon, Feta and Mint
recipes.blurb: Three ingredients, no cooking, and the most refreshing thing on a hot table. Ten minutes with a knife.
steps: Cube the watermelon and drain it in a colander for 5 minutes. Skipping this gives you pink soup by the time it reaches the table.
Spread on a wide platter — not a deep bowl.
Scatter feta, mint and cucumber. Squeeze the lime over, drizzle the oil, and grind a lot of black pepper across the top.
Serve within 30 minutes.
recipes.kidTweak: Plain watermelon on the side. Nobody has ever needed to be sold on plain watermelon.
recipes.restaurantTouch: The black pepper. It sounds wrong on fruit and it is what makes people ask.
recipes.garden: Mint from the pot; watermelon if you have the room and the patience.
recipes.leftovers: Same day only.

recipes.title: Big-Batch Baked Ziti with White Beans
recipes.blurb: Feeds twelve, travels in the dish you baked it in, and reheats without complaint. The potluck workhorse.
steps: Boil the pasta 2 minutes short of al dente — it finishes in the oven, and fully cooked pasta here turns to mush.
Cook the onion in oil 7 minutes; add garlic, oregano and pepper flakes for a minute; fry the tomato paste 90 seconds until it darkens.
Add crushed tomatoes, one can of beans and the salt. Simmer 10 minutes. Blend the second can of beans with 1/2 cup water until smooth and stir it in — that is the creaminess, without cream.
Wilt the spinach into the sauce. Mix the ricotta with the egg, half the parmesan and plenty of pepper.
Layer in a 9x13: sauce, pasta, dollops of ricotta, mozzarella. Repeat. Finish with the rest of the parmesan.
Bake at 375°F for 30 minutes covered, 15 uncovered until bubbling and browned. Rest 15 minutes before cutting, and scatter basil over.

omnivore.label: Add browned sausage or turkey
omnivore.note: Brown separately, and stir into half the sauce if you need both versions in one dish.
steps: Brown with a pinch of fennel seed and oregano, and fold into half the sauce.

recipes.kidTweak: This is the meal children request. If yours object to spinach, blend it into the sauce with the beans and it vanishes.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Rest it a full 15 minutes. Baked pasta cut straight from the oven slumps onto the plate; rested, it holds a square.
recipes.garden: Basil, and tomatoes if you cook down your own sauce in September.
recipes.leftovers: 5 days. Freezes 3 months baked or unbaked.
recipes.prepAhead: Assemble up to two days ahead unbaked. From the fridge, add 15 minutes covered.

recipes.title: Seven-Layer Bean Dip
recipes.blurb: The game-day dish that people stand around. Built on real refried beans and Greek yogurt instead of sour cream, and nobody can tell.
steps: Blend the pinto beans with cumin, smoked paprika, chipotle, the juice of one lime, the oil and 2 tbsp water until spreadable. Spread in the bottom of a glass dish so the layers show.
Mash the avocados with the second lime and salt; spread over the beans, right to the edges so they do not brown.
Spread the yogurt, then the drained salsa. Draining matters — undrained salsa turns the whole thing into a puddle by halftime.
Cheese, tomatoes, scallions, olives, cilantro.
Refrigerate up to 4 hours. Serve with sturdy chips or cut vegetables.
recipes.kidTweak: Skip the chipotle in the beans and keep one corner plain beans-cheese-chips.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Use a straight-sided glass dish. Half the appeal of this thing is being able to see the layers.
recipes.garden: Tomatoes, scallions and cilantro.
recipes.leftovers: 2 days, though the avocado layer dulls. Best made the day of.

recipes.title: Buffalo Cauliflower Bites
recipes.blurb: Crisp, hot, and gone in ten minutes. Roasted rather than fried, so you can eat a plateful without regret.
steps: Heat oven to 450°F. Whisk flour, milk, garlic powder and smoked paprika into a thin batter.
Toss the florets to coat, letting the excess drip off, and spread on two oiled pans with space between them. Crowding steams them.
Bake 22 minutes until the coating is set and dry.

Whisk sriracha, melted butter, vinegar and the canola oil. Toss the hot cauliflower in it and return to the oven for 8 minutes — sauce on at the end, so it bakes onto the surface instead of soaking in.
Blend yogurt with feta for a blue-cheese-style dip. Serve with celery, carrots and scallions.
recipes.kidTweak: Pull a tray of plain baked florets before the sauce. They are basically cauliflower nuggets.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Two pans, not one. The single most common reason home roasted vegetables are soft is that they were crowded.
recipes.garden: Fall cauliflower, if you transplanted in August.
recipes.leftovers: Best hot. Re-crisp in a hot oven, never a microwave.

recipes.title: Mediterranean Orzo Salad
recipes.blurb: Makes a bowl the size of a punchbowl, travels in a cooler, and is better an hour after you make it. The default potluck contribution.
steps: Cook the orzo in well-salted water to just al dente, drain, and rinse under cold water until cool. Rinsing is right here even though it is wrong for hot pasta — it stops the cooking and removes the starch that would glue the salad together.
Toss the warm-but-not-hot orzo with 2 tbsp of the oil so it stays loose.
Whisk the remaining oil, lemon, vinegar, Dijon, oregano and pepper.
Fold everything together except the feta and herbs. Let it sit 20 minutes — the orzo drinks the dressing, which is why this needs more dressing than you think.
Fold in feta, parsley and dill just before serving. Taste and add lemon; it almost always wants more.

omnivore.label: Add grilled chicken or shrimp
omnivore.note: Sliced cold over the top, or folded through half the bowl.
steps: Marinate in lemon, oregano and oil, grill, slice and fold in.

recipes.kidTweak: Fill a small container with plain buttered orzo, cucumber and feta before you dress the big bowl.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Herbs at the end, in quantity. A cup of parsley is not a garnish, it is an ingredient.
recipes.garden: Cucumbers, tomatoes, parsley and dill all at once in July.
recipes.leftovers: 4 days. Add a squeeze of lemon before serving again — it flattens overnight.
recipes.prepAhead: Make it the morning of. It genuinely wants an hour.

recipes.title: Olive Oil Banana Bread
recipes.blurb: Moister than the butter version and it keeps better, which is exactly what a bake sale needs. One bowl, no mixer.
steps: Heat oven to 350°F and line a loaf pan. Use bananas that look ruined — black skins, soft to the touch. Underripe bananas are the reason most banana bread is bland.
Mash the bananas in a big bowl, then whisk in oil, applesauce, brown sugar, eggs and vanilla.
Add both flours, baking soda, baking powder, cinnamon and salt on top. Fold until barely combined — lumps are fine, overmixing makes it tough.
Fold in walnuts and chocolate chips if using. Scrape into the pan.
Bake 55-65 minutes until a skewer in the center comes out with a few damp crumbs. Tent with foil at 40 minutes if it is browning fast.
Cool in the pan 15 minutes, then completely on a rack before slicing. It slices cleanly cold and messily warm.
recipes.kidTweak: This is the recipe to hand over entirely. Mashing bananas is the best job in the kitchen and there is nothing sharp or hot until the pan goes in.
recipes.restaurantTouch: A scattering of turbinado sugar over the batter before baking gives a crackly top worth a dollar more at the table.
recipes.garden: None.
recipes.leftovers: 4 days wrapped, 3 months frozen. Slice before freezing and take one out at a time.
recipes.prepAhead: Bakes the night before a sale and is better for it.

recipes.title: Chewy Oatmeal Cookies
recipes.blurb: Crisp edge, chewy middle, actual oat flavor. They travel well and they sell out first.
steps: Beat the butter, oil and both sugars for 2 full minutes until pale and fluffy. This is where the texture comes from, and 30 seconds is not enough.
Beat in the egg and vanilla.
Fold in flour, baking soda, cinnamon and salt, then the oats, raisins and pecans. The dough will look barely held together — correct.
Chill the dough 30 minutes. Cold dough spreads less and browns better.
Scoop golf-ball portions onto lined pans, well apart, and bake at 350°F for 10-12 minutes. Pull them when the centers still look underdone; they set on the pan.
Cool on the pan 5 minutes before moving. The chew depends on this.
recipes.kidTweak: Scooping and eating a little raw dough is most of the appeal. Use pasteurised eggs if that matters to you.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Flaky salt on top of each cookie before baking.
recipes.garden: None.
recipes.leftovers: 5 days in a tin. The dough freezes as scooped balls for 3 months — bake from frozen, adding 2 minutes.

recipes.title: Dark Chocolate Olive Oil Brownies
recipes.blurb: Fudgy, glossy-topped, and made with olive oil instead of a stick of butter. Nobody guesses.
steps: Heat oven to 350°F and line an 8x8 pan with parchment, leaving overhangs.
Whisk the oil, both sugars and cocoa together first and let it sit 5 minutes. Blooming the cocoa in fat is what makes the chocolate taste deep instead of dusty.
Whisk in the eggs one at a time, then the vanilla, and beat hard for a full minute — that vigorous whisking is what gives brownies their papery, glossy top.
Fold in flour and salt until just combined, then the chocolate chips and walnuts.
Bake 25-28 minutes. The center should still wobble slightly; a clean skewer means you have gone too far.
Cool completely in the pan before lifting out and cutting. Warm brownies cut into rubble.
recipes.kidTweak: Nothing needed. This is the recipe children request by name.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Flaky salt over the top the moment it leaves the oven.
recipes.garden: None.
recipes.leftovers: 4 days in a tin, 3 months frozen. They are excellent cold, straight from the fridge.

recipes.title: Overnight Baked French Toast
recipes.blurb: Assembled the night before, baked while people open presents. Feeds eight and makes the house smell like a holiday.
steps: Butter or oil a 9x13 and pack in the bread cubes and berries.
Whisk eggs, whites, milk, maple, vanilla, cinnamon and salt until completely uniform, and pour over. Press the bread down so every piece is soaked.
Cover and refrigerate overnight — at least 4 hours. This is not a shortcut you can skip; the custard has to get inside the bread.
In the morning, scatter the pecans over and bake uncovered at 350°F for 45-50 minutes until puffed and set in the middle.
Rest 10 minutes. Serve with yogurt and a little more maple.
recipes.kidTweak: Kids can tear the bread and scatter the berries the night before. It is the ideal Christmas Eve job.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Slightly stale bread. Fresh bread turns to pudding; day-old bread holds its shape and gives you edges.
recipes.garden: Summer berries, frozen in July for exactly this.
recipes.leftovers: 3 days. Reheat squares in a hot oven.

recipes.title: Fifteen-Minute Chickpea Skillet
recipes.blurb: Pantry to plate in the time it takes to set the table. No chopping board required if you buy the spinach pre-washed.
steps: Start the garlic in cold oil over medium with the pepper flakes. By the time it sizzles and turns pale gold, about 3 minutes, the flavor is in the oil.
Add cumin, smoked paprika and tomato paste; fry 60 seconds until it darkens.
Add chickpeas and tomatoes with the salt. Simmer hard for 6 minutes, smashing about a third of the chickpeas against the pan so the sauce thickens.
Stir in the spinach until it wilts, 1 minute. Finish with lemon juice.
Spoon over toast with a dollop of yogurt. Dinner, from a cupboard, in a quarter of an hour.
recipes.kidTweak: Skip the pepper flakes and serve over rice or pasta instead of toast.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Smashing a third of the chickpeas. It takes ten seconds and turns a loose pan of beans into a sauce that clings.
recipes.garden: Spinach in spring and autumn.
recipes.leftovers: 4 days, and it thickens into something you can put in a wrap.

recipes.title: Ten-Minute Egg Fried Rice
recipes.blurb: The reason to cook extra rice. Leftover rice, frozen peas, eggs, and dinner is done before anyone asks what's for dinner.
steps: Cold rice is mandatory. Fresh rice steams and clumps; day-old rice fries. If you only have fresh, spread it on a tray in the freezer for 15 minutes.
Scramble the eggs in 1 tbsp oil over high heat, 45 seconds, until just set. Tip them out.
Add the second tablespoon of oil, then the carrots for 2 minutes, then garlic and ginger for 30 seconds.
Add the rice and press it into the pan. Leave it alone for a full minute to catch, then toss. Repeat twice — those crisp bits are the whole point.
Add peas, edamame, the eggs back, soy sauce and pepper; toss 1 minute. Off heat: sesame oil and scallions.

omnivore.label: Add leftover chicken or shrimp
omnivore.note: Anything already cooked goes in with the peas.
steps: Add with the peas and toss until heated through.

recipes.kidTweak: This is already most kids' favorite thing. Serve theirs before the pepper.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Get the pan hotter than feels sensible and let the rice sit still. Restaurant fried rice tastes different because of heat and patience, not ingredients.
recipes.garden: Scallions and carrots.
recipes.leftovers: Eat it now. Twice-fried rice is not a thing.

recipes.title: White Bean Melt
recipes.blurb: Twelve minutes, mostly under the broiler. Crunchy, savory, melty, and built entirely from things already in the cupboard.
steps: Mash the beans roughly with the yogurt, Dijon, lemon and pepper — leave some whole for texture.
Fold in celery, red onion, capers and dill.
Toast the bread on a sheet pan under the broiler for 90 seconds a side.
Pile the bean mixture on, top with tomato and cheese, and broil 2-3 minutes until the cheese blisters. Watch it — broilers go from perfect to charcoal in about twenty seconds.
Eat immediately with a knife and fork.

omnivore.label: Make it a tuna melt
omnivore.note: A drained can of tuna folded into half the mixture is the classic.
steps: Fold into half the bean mixture and build those two sandwiches separately.

recipes.kidTweak: Skip the capers and onion, cut into fingers.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Rinsed capers. A tablespoon adds the briny pop people cannot identify but always notice.
recipes.garden: Dill and tomatoes.
recipes.leftovers: The bean salad keeps 3 days; assemble to order.

recipes.title: Loaded Sweet Potato, Two Ways
recipes.blurb: Microwave a sweet potato, open a can, and it is dinner. The lowest-effort real meal in the collection.
steps: Prick the sweet potatoes all over, microwave 8-12 minutes turning once, until completely soft. Finish under a broiler for 4 minutes if you want the skin to crisp.
Warm the beans in the oil with cumin and smoked paprika, 4 minutes, smashing some against the pan.
Split each potato and fluff the inside with a fork.
SOUTHWEST: beans, salsa, avocado, yogurt, cilantro, lime.
MEDITERRANEAN: chickpeas instead of black beans, tahini thinned with lemon, parsley, a pinch of za'atar.
Either way, squeeze citrus over at the end.
recipes.kidTweak: Plain potato, butter, cheese. Still counts.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Broil the microwaved potato for four minutes. It gives you the crisp skin the microwave cannot.
recipes.garden: Sweet potatoes store for months from an autumn harvest.
recipes.leftovers: Cooked potatoes keep 4 days and reheat well.

recipes.title: Spring Pea and Asparagus Tart
recipes.blurb: Green, elegant, and mostly assembly. It looks like it took all morning and takes forty minutes.
steps: Heat oven to 425°F. Roll the dough to a rectangle on parchment and score a one-inch border without cutting through.
Blend the ricotta with the goat cheese, lemon zest, half the salt and plenty of pepper until smooth. Spread inside the border.
Crush half the peas roughly and scatter with the whole peas, asparagus and scallions. Drizzle with 2 tbsp oil, season.
Brush the border with egg and bake 22-25 minutes until the crust is deep golden and the asparagus is tender.
Finish with mint, the last of the oil, and a handful of arugula. Cut into squares — warm or at room temperature both work.
recipes.kidTweak: Leave a quarter of the tart with just cheese, no green things.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Crushing half the peas. It gives you two textures from one ingredient and makes the surface look considered.
recipes.garden: Asparagus in late April and peas in June are the two crops that announce spring here.
recipes.leftovers: 2 days. Re-crisp in the oven; do not microwave a tart.

recipes.title: Whipped Feta with Hot Honey and Pistachios
recipes.blurb: Feta and yogurt beaten until it turns into something closer to a cloud, then flooded with warm chile honey. It takes eight minutes and it is always the first bowl to empty.
steps: Put the feta, yogurt, olive oil, lemon juice and zest, garlic clove and pepper in a food processor and run it for a full 2 minutes, scraping down twice.
Two minutes is longer than feels necessary and it is the whole recipe. Under-processed it is a dip; properly whipped it is aerated and holds a swoosh.
Warm the honey with the pepper flakes in a small pan or 20 seconds in the microwave, just enough to loosen it and let the chile bloom.
Spread the whipped feta across a shallow plate with the back of a spoon, leaving ridges. Ridges catch honey; a flat surface lets it run to the edge.
Pour the hot honey over the middle, scatter the pistachios and mint, and serve with warm pita.
recipes.kidTweak: Leave the pepper flakes out of half the honey. Plain honey over whipped feta with pita is a genuinely good kid snack — it reads as cream cheese.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Chill the plate first. The honey sets slightly where it hits the cold feta and stays in a pool instead of sliding off.
recipes.garden: Mint is unstoppable here — grow it in a sunken pot so it cannot run. One plant covers a summer of this.
recipes.leftovers: The whipped feta keeps 5 days and firms up in the fridge; let it sit out 20 minutes and stir before serving. Add honey fresh each time.
recipes.prepAhead: Whip it up to two days ahead. Assembly at the party is 60 seconds.

recipes.title: Skillet Garlic Bread with a Parmesan Crust
recipes.blurb: Garlic butter worked into a split baguette, then the cut face pressed into parmesan and crisped in a skillet until it forms a lacy golden crust. It is not the garlic bread from the freezer aisle.
steps: Mash the softened butter with the grated garlic, parsley, pepper flakes, salt and lemon zest. Use raw grated garlic, not powder — the point of this is that it is sharp.
Spread it thickly over both cut faces of the baguette, right to the edges.
Scatter the parmesan over a plate and press each buttered face down into it so the cheese sticks in a solid layer.
Heat the olive oil in a large skillet over medium. Lay the halves cheese side down and press them flat with a spatula or a second pan.
Cook 4-6 minutes without moving them. You are waiting for the parmesan to melt, then fry, then set into a crust. Lift a corner at 4 minutes to check — it should be lace-patterned and deep gold.
Flip and warm the crust side 2 minutes. Cut into thick pieces with a serrated knife and serve immediately, cheese side up.
recipes.kidTweak: Skip the pepper flakes and cut it into short fingers. This disappears faster than anything else at a table with kids at it.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Finish with a scatter of parmesan and parsley over the hot crust the moment it comes out of the pan, so a little melts and the rest stays raw and green.
recipes.garden: Flat-leaf parsley is a biennial that overwinters here under mulch and gives you an early spring crop before anything else is up.
recipes.leftovers: Best within the hour. Leftovers make excellent croutons — cube them and toast at 375°F for 8 minutes.

recipes.title: Salted Tahini Chocolate Chip Cookies
recipes.blurb: Tahini gives these the savory, slightly bitter edge that makes a chocolate chip cookie interesting instead of just sweet. Flaky salt on top, and the middles stay soft for days.
steps: Beat the butter, tahini and both sugars together for a full 3 minutes until pale and fluffy. Stir the tahini in its jar first — the separated oil on top is not optional to mix back in.
Beat in the egg and vanilla until smooth.
Whisk both flours, baking soda and salt in a separate bowl, then fold them in until just combined. Stop the moment the flour disappears.
Fold in the chopped chocolate. Chopping a bar rather than using chips gives you shards and puddles instead of uniform dots, which is most of the difference between a homemade cookie and a store one.
Chill the dough at least 45 minutes, or overnight. Cold dough spreads less and browns better, and the flavor deepens noticeably by the next day.
Heat the oven to 350°F. Scoop rounded tablespoons onto lined sheets, well apart. Press a few sesame seeds and a pinch of flaky salt onto each top.

Bake 10-12 minutes, until the edges are set and the middles still look slightly underdone. They finish on the hot pan. A cookie baked until the center looks done is a cookie that will be hard by evening.
Cool on the pan 5 minutes before moving them.
recipes.kidTweak: Tahini tastes faintly of sesame and nothing else — most kids never identify it. Skip the flaky salt on a few if that is a sticking point.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Bang the sheet pan on the counter once at the 8-minute mark. It collapses the rising center and gives you those concentric ripple rings bakeries charge extra for.
recipes.garden: Nothing here grows in a garden, which is the honest answer. This is a pantry recipe and it is the one to make in February when there is nothing to harvest.
recipes.leftovers: Keeps 5 days in a tin with a slice of bread to hold the moisture. Scooped dough balls freeze 3 months and bake from frozen with 2 extra minutes.
recipes.prepAhead: Make the dough up to 3 days ahead. It genuinely improves on day two.

recipes.title: Skillet Peach and Blueberry Crumble
recipes.blurb: August peaches cooked down in the same pan they are baked in, under a buttery oat topping that stays crunchy. It goes in the oven while you eat and comes out at exactly the right moment.
steps: Heat the oven to 375°F. Toss the peaches and blueberries in the skillet with the brown sugar, cornstarch, lemon juice, cinnamon and vanilla. Leave the skins on the peaches — they hold the slices together and they turn a good color.
Let the fruit sit 10 minutes. It will draw out juice, which the cornstarch then thickens into a sauce rather than a puddle.
Rub the oats, whole wheat flour, almonds, salt and cold butter together with your fingers until it clumps in pieces the size of peas and hazelnuts. Uneven is right — uniform crumble bakes into a lid.
Drizzle the maple over the crumble mixture and toss once with a fork. That is what makes the clusters crisp rather than sandy.
Scatter it over the fruit, leaving gaps so the juices can bubble up through.
Bake 35-40 minutes, until the topping is deep golden and the fruit is bubbling thickly at the edges — not just steaming. Thin bubbles mean the starch has not set yet.
Rest 15 minutes before serving. Straight out of the oven it will run everywhere. With cold yogurt or ice cream.
recipes.kidTweak: Peel the peaches for a texture-sensitive kid and leave out the almonds — the crumble works fine without them.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Serve it in the skillet at the table with a spoon stuck in it. Nobody has ever been disappointed by a cast-iron pan arriving still bubbling.
recipes.garden: Ohio peaches from an orchard in August are worth planning around. Blueberries do well in containers here with acidic potting mix — two bushes will cover this and breakfast.
recipes.leftovers: Keeps 3 days covered. The topping softens; 10 minutes in a 350°F oven brings it back. Excellent cold for breakfast with yogurt, which is not a joke.
